'''''Eucalyptus diversicolor''''', commonly known as '''karri''',<ref name="FloraBase" /> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Myrtaceae]] and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[Southwest Australia|south-west]] of [[Western Australia]]. It is a tall tree with smooth light grey to cream-coloured, often mottled bark, lance-shaped adult leaves and barrel-shaped fruit. Found in higher rainfall areas, karri is commercially important for its timber.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' is the tallest tree that grows in Western Australia.<ref name=CALM/> It is a tall forest tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|10–60|m}}<ref name=anps>{{cite web|url=https://anpsa.org.au/plant_profiles/eucalyptus-diversicolor/|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society}}</ref> but can reach as high as {{cvt|90|m}},<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|id=5625}}</ref> making it the tallest tree in Western Australia and one of the tallest in the world.<ref name=AG>{{cite web|url=http://www.australiangeographic.com.au/topics/science-environment/2014/07/australias-tallest-trees-are-karris|title=Searching for Australia's tallest trees: Karris|author=Karen McGhee|date=2 July 2014|access-date=3 December 2017|publisher=[[Australian Geographic]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.inspirationoutdoors.com.au/bibbulmun-track-pemberton-to-northcliffe-karris-and-koalas-ok-no-koalas/|title=What's in a Name? ''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' on the Bibbulmun Track, Pemberton to Northcliffe|date=5 February 2013|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=Inspiration Outdoors}}</ref><ref name=Stanford>{{cite web|url=https://trees.stanford.edu/ENCYC/EUCdiv.htm|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' karri Myrtaceae (myrtle family)|access-date=2 December 2017|work=Trees of Stanford|publisher=[[Stanford University]]}}</ref> As of February 2019, the tallest known living karri is just over {{cvt|80|m}} tall. A tree south of Pemberton, known as 'The Tyrant' is {{cvt|69|m}} tall and {{cvt|11.5|m}} in girth and contains approximately {{cvt|220|m3}} of wood in its trunk and is thought to be the largest karri by wood volume.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nicolle |first1=Dean |title=Eucalypts of Western Australia - The South West Coast and Ranges |date=2019 |publisher=Scott Print |location=WA |isbn=978-0-646-80613-6 |pages=260–1 |edition=1st}}</ref> A ''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' of {{cvt|72.9|m}} height and of {{cvt|5.71|m}} girth in [[Coimbra]], Portugal, is the tallest reliably measured tree in Europe.<ref>Karri 'Karri Knight' in the Valle de Canas, Valle de Canas, Centro, Portugal, MonumentalTrees.com https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/prt/centro/coimbra/4104_valledecanas/8314/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227101558/https://www.monumentaltrees.com/en/prt/centro/coimbra/4104_valledecanas/8314/|date=27 December 2019}}</ref>

Karri do not form a [[lignotuber]] but do form [[epicormic]] buds located under the bark along the length of the stem.<ref name=euclid/>

The bark on the trunk and branches is smooth, grey to cream-coloured or pale orange, often mottled and is shed in larger plates, short ribbons or small polygonal flakes.<ref name="nsw" /><ref name="Euclid">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_diversicolor.htm |publisher=Euclid: Eucalypts of Australia |access-date=28 January 2021}}</ref> The bark sheds each year with the new white bark contrasting with the orange to yellow new bark contrasts against the recently exposed white bark. The bark becomes increasingly granulated with age.<ref name=euclid/> The bark is rich in [[tannin]]s.<ref name=gardner>{{cite web|url=https://library.dpird.wa.gov.au/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1013&context=journal_agriculture3|title=Trees of W.A. Jarrah and Karri|author=[[Charles Austin Gardner]]|work=Journal of the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia, series 3 |volume=1|number=1|date=1 February 1952|access-date=20 December 2023|publisher=[[Department of Agriculture (Western Australia)|Department of Agriculture]]}}</ref>

The stems and branchlets are round in cross section, the branchlets have no oil glands in the pith.<ref name=euclid/>

The leaves on young plants and on [[coppice]] regrowth are arranged in opposite pairs, broadly egg-shaped to almost round, paler on the lower surface, {{cvt|50–155|mm}} long, {{cvt|25–100|mm}} wide and [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]]. The leaves tend to be more spreading than pendulous.<ref name=gardner/> Adult leaves are arranged alternately, glossy dark green on the upper surface, paler below, lance-shaped, {{cvt|70–135|mm}} long and {{cvt|15–37|mm}} wide on a flattened or channelled petiole {{cvt|10–20|mm}} long. The leaves are penniveined, where the veins arise pinnately, in a feather like arrangement, from a single primary vein. The leaves are [[Leaf#Venation|densely reticulated]] where the network of veins within the leaf is packed closely together. The prominent vein near the margin of the leaf is very close to the margin and runs almost parallel with it. The yellow oil glands within the leaves are situated in centre of the smallest unreticulated areas.<ref name=euclid/> The fine lateral nerves spread at a wide angle from the midrib.<ref name=gardner/>

The unbranched [[inflorescence]]s are situated in the [[axil]]s in small clusters on a common stalk. The flower buds are arranged in groups of seven in leaf axils on a rounded [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|12–30|mm}} long, each bud on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|3–6|mm}} long. The buds are oval, {{cvt|11–16|mm}} long and {{cvt|5–7|mm}} wide at maturity with a conical [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering has been observed in January, April, May, August and December, and the flowers are white.<ref name=euclid/> The flowers have narrow cylindrical [[Sepal|calyx]] tubes that slowly taper to the base into the pedicel. The many stamen form a continuous ring and has inflected white coloured filaments. The [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] at the end of the filaments have an oblong shape and open into a parallel longitudinal slits.<ref name=gardner/>

The fruit is a woody barrel-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|10–12|mm}} long and {{cvt|8–10|mm}} wide on a pedicel {{cvt|5–6|mm}} long with three valves at or below rim level.<ref name="nsw" /><ref name="Euclid" />

The seeds found within the fruits have a flattened ovoid shape, are grey in colour with a length of {{cvt|1.2|to|3|mm}}. The seeds are pointed at one end with a smooth back and a scar from where it was once attached to the placenta on the underside.<ref name=euclid/>

The species has a [[haploid]] [[chromosome]] number of 12.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://treegenesdb.org/org/Eucalyptus-diversicolor|title=Eucalyptus diversicolor|access-date=21 December 2023|publisher=TreeGenes}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' was first formally described in 1863 by the [[botanist]] [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] in his book ''[[Fragmenta Phytographiae Australiae]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454962|publisher=APNI|access-date=29 January 2021}}</ref><ref name="F.Muell.">{{cite book |last1=von Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Fragmenta Phytographiae Australiae |volume=3|date=1863 |publisher=Victorian Government Printer |location=Melbourne |pages=131–132 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/7220#page/139/mode/1up |access-date=29 January 2021}}</ref> The type specimen was collected in 1860 by the [[botanist]] [[Augustus Frederick Oldfield]] near [[Wilson Inlet]]; the location given, in Latin, is ''In Australiae regionibus depressioribus quam Maxime austro occidentalibus''.<ref name=nsw>{{cite web|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_diversicolor.htm?zoom_highlight=Eucalyptus+diversicolor|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|access-date=5 March 2026|work=Eucalink|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Sydney}}</ref><ref name="F.Muell." />

The [[holotype]] is held at [[Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria]], [[syntype]]s are held at [[Cambridge University Herbarium]], [[Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh]] and [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref name=euclid>{{cite web|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_diversicolor.htm|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' Karri|access-date=21 December 2023|year=2020|work=Euclid Eucalypts of Australia Fourth Edition|publisher=[[CSIRO]]}}</ref>

The botanical name ''diversicolor'' is taken from the [[Latin]] word ''diversus'' meaning to turn apart and color or "separate colours" and refers to the difference between the top of the leaf and its underside.<ref name=anps/><ref name=euclid/>
The common name is derived from the [[Noongar]] name for the tree ''karri'' pronounced ''ka-ree''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bgpa.wa.gov.au/kings-park/visit/history/2-uncategorised|title=Nyoongar Words and Definitions|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=Kings Park & Botanic Garden}}</ref>

Karri is a part of the ''Symphyomyrtus'' subgenus, all of which have two opercula on the buds and have four rows of ovules. It is not closely related to any other members of the subgenus and is the sole species in the section ''Inclusae''. The defining feature of this section is having inflexed stamens, flattened ovoid seed shape, enclosed valves of the fruit and the lack of pith glands in the branchlets. Although it has no closely related species it has some affinity with tall Eucalypts found the wet forests of eastern Australian including ''[[Eucalyptus saligna|E.{{nbsp}}saligna]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus grandis|E.{{nbsp}}grandis]]'' all of which have discolorous adult leaves and seeds with a flattened-ovoid shape.<ref name=euclid/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Eucalyptus diversicolor distribution.png|thumb|right|Distribution]]
The climate over the range of the tree is mildly temperate with small variations in humidity and temperature with frosts only occurring on rare occasions.<ref name=CALM/>
Karri occurs only within the [[High Rainfall Zone]] of the [[South West Botanical Province]] of [[Western Australia]] which receives {{convert|900|to|1300|mm|in|1}} of rain per year, mostly in winter.<ref name=fpc>{{cite web archived|url=http://www.fpc.wa.gov.au/node/841|title=Karri ''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=Forest Products Commission|archive-date=15 September 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> It mostly occurs within the [[Warren (biogeographic region)|Warren]] biogeographic region, but there are some outlying populations including the [[Porongorup Ranges]], [[Mount Manypeaks]], [[Torbay, Western Australia|Torbay]], [[Rocky Gully, Western Australia|Rocky Gully]] all along the south coast and [[Karridale, Western Australia|Karridale]] and Forest Grove to the north west<ref name=fpc/> and the Leeuwin-Naturaliste Ridge to the south of [[Margaret River, Western Australia|Margaret River]] to the west of the main belt.<ref name=gondwana/>

The heart of the karri forest is found near [[Nannup, Western Australia|Nannup]] and [[Manjimup, Western Australia|Manjimup]] through to [[Denmark, Western Australia|Denmark]].<ref name=gondwana>{{cite web|url=http://www.gondwanalink.org/natwonders/karri.aspx|title=Karri Forests|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=GondwanaLink|year=2014}}</ref>

The total area covered by karri forest is less than {{convert|200000|ha|acre|0}} which is about one fifth of its virgin growth.<ref name=AG/> The nearest tall tree forests are some {{convert|3000|km|mi|0}} to the east in [[Tasmania]] and [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]].<ref name=AG/>

Karri has been introduced to parts of Africa including; [[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]] and the [[Canary Islands]].<ref name=kew>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A592885-1|title=''Eucalyptus diversicolor'' F.Muell.|access-date=20 December 2023|work=Plants of the World Online|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref>

The species is considered invasive in South Africa where it is a problem in the [[Western Cape]] region and is locally known a ''karie''. It commonly invades clearings, fynbos, water courses and road sides often out competing local species and is spread easily by seed dispersal.<ref name=Invasive>{{cite web|url=http://www.invasives.org.za/legislation/item/251-karri-eucalyptus-diversicolor|title=Karri ''Eucalyptus diversicolor''|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=Invasive Species South Africa}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
Karri is regarded as one of the six forest giants found in Western Australia; the others being ''[[Corymbia calophylla]]'' (marri), ''[[Eucalyptus gomphocephala]]'' (tuart), ''[[Eucalyptus jacksonii]]'' (red tingle), ''[[Eucalyptus marginata]]'' (jarrah) and ''[[Eucalyptus patens]]'' (yarri).<ref name=seed>{{cite web|url=https://australianseed.com/shop/item/eucalyptus-gomphocephala|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala''|access-date=22 August 2017|publisher=Australian Seed}}</ref><ref name=pfaf>{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/User/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Eucalyptus+gomphocephala|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala''|access-date=28 April 2023|publisher=Plants For A Future}}</ref>

Some karri specimens are thought to reach an age of up to 300 years.<ref name=AG/> The soil in which the species grows is often poor, and the tree tends to flower after fire to take advantage of the nutrients released by the combustion of forest litter. The soil is classified as karri loam. Though low in some minor nutrients it is admired for its depth and pasture-growing properties. The depth of the soil is several metres and thought to be created primarily from the bark shed by the tree, which collects at the trunk base to a depth upwards of six metres in mature trees. The karri supports an extensive ecosystem which is connected to the granite outcrops of the lower south-west and the many subsequent creeks and rivers created from runoff. Karri generally dominate in the deep valleys between granite outcrops surrounding the creeks and rivers.

A dense [[understorey]] is found in karri forest areas which retains moisture over the hot summers. Associated trees and shrubs found in the understorey include the peppermint (''[[Agonis flexuosa]]''), karri sheoak (''[[Allocasuarina decussata]]''), karri wattle (''[[Acacia pentadenia]]'') and karri oak (''[[Chorilaena quercifolia]]''). A diverse assemblage of flowers and smaller plants – around 2,000 plant taxa – make up the mosaic of habitats within the karri forests.<ref name=gondwana/>

The tree has a complex floral cycle and it takes four to five years from the production of flowers to the seeds being released. The production of seed is dependent on a multitude of variables including tree density, availability of pollinators, soil moisture, genetics, nutrients and fire.<ref name=CALM>{{cite web|url=https://library.dbca.wa.gov.au/static/Journals/080273/080273-02.003.pdf|title=A review of silvicultural research in the karri ''(Eucalyptus diversicolor)'' forest|author1=R.Breidahl|author2=P.J.Hewett|work=CALMScience|year=1995|publisher=Department of Conservation and Land Management}}</ref>

===Pollinators===
Most Eucalypts achieve pollination through insects and birds rather than wind. Insects are far less active through the colder winter months so bird pollination is thought to be more important. The trees are often visited by nectar feeding birds, particularly [[Purple-crowned lorikeet]]s. The lorikeets have a wide range and are quite active during winter and are thought to be dominant pollinators and able to cross pollinate over larger distances.<ref name=CALM/>
Karri is a source of [[pollen]] for honeybees (''[[Apis mellifera]]''). The pollen has a protein content of 23.4% and provides sufficient [[amino acid]]s for the  nutrition of ''A.{{nbsp}}mellifera''. The content of some of the amino acids are; 3.84% [[proline]], 2.07% [[glutamic acid]], 1.72% [[lysine]], 1.22% [[cystine]], 1.91% [[aspartic acid]], 1.50% [[leucine]], 1.11% [[alanine]] and 1.11% [[valine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://agrifutures.com.au/wp-content/uploads/publications/01-053.pdf|title=Pollen analysis of Eucalypts in Western Australia - A report for the Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation|access-date=20 December 2023|author=Rob Manning|date=1 May 2001|publisher=Rural Industries Research and Development Corporation}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Deanmill karri logs on train.jpg|thumb|[[Deanmill, Western Australia|Deanmill]] karri logs on train]]
[[File:Karri log in Primer of Forestry Poole 1922.png|thumb|'Log and fallers.' Poole, C. E. L., ''Primer of Forestry'' 1922]]
The wood has a green [[density]] of around {{convert|1200|kg/m3|lb/cuft|0}} with an air-dried density of about {{convert|900|kg/m3|lb/cuft|0}}.<ref name=fpc/> 
The [[heartwood]] of Karri is a red colour and closely resembles [[jarrah]] heartwood. Bushmen used to tell the two timbers apart by burning a splint of wood, Karri would leave a white ash and jarrah would leave a grey to black coloured ash.<ref name=gardner/> Timber from Karri is suitable for construction work. It is a little more dense than jarrah but is much stronger. Karri wood is not as [[termite]] resistant as that of jarrah.<ref name=gardner/>
The tree has been logged since the settlement of Western Australia with logging towns appearing throughout the range of the tree and producing hardwood timbers, mostly for construction purposes, for the first 150 years since settlement.<ref name=gondwana/> The first Karri timber to be felled for export was at the isolated population around Leeuwin, which became known as Karridale. The virtues of the wood were promoted in the 1920s by the state conservator of forests, [[Charles Lane-Poole]], who noted the colonists' preference for other timber as its vulnerability to white ants made it a poor choice for fence posts and railway sleepers. The timber found uses in the state for wagon spokes and wooden pipes, and in England it was found suitable for [[scantling]]s by the national railway and telegraph arms by the postal services and was listed among [[Lloyd's Register|Lloyds]] shipbuilding timbers as possessing great strength over large lengths.<ref name="Lane-Poole1922">{{cite book |last1=Lane-Poole |first1=C. E. |author-link1=Charles Lane-Poole |title=A primer of forestry, with illustrations of the principal forest trees of Western Australia. |url=https://archive.org/details/primerofforestry00lane |date=1922 |publisher=F.W. Simpson, government printer |location=Perth |page=[https://archive.org/details/primerofforestry00lane/page/44 44] |language=en|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.61019 |hdl=2027/uiug.30112041668135 }}</ref>

[[Lookout tree|Fire lookouts]] were established in the forests using the tallest Karri trees, giving the foresters a commanding view of the landscape.
The idea of using karri trees in this way was first suggested in 1937 by a young forester, Don Stewart, who later became Conservator of Forests. The first of these was built on a large marri (''[[Corymbia calophylla]]'') at Alco, near [[Nannup, Western Australia|Nannup]]. Eight lookouts were established in the forests between 1937 and 1952. [[Spotter plane]]s are now used and some of the trees are now used as tourist attractions.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dn.com.au/Big_Famous_Trees_gallery/pages/Diamond-Tree-Eucalyptus-diversicolor-karri.html|title=Diamond Tree|work=Big and Famous Trees gallery|author=Dean Nicolle|publisher=[[Currency Creek Arboretum]]|access-date=2 December 2017|author-link=Dean Nicolle}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.trusttrees.org.au/tree/WA/Pemberton/Gloucester_National_Park|title=Gloucester tree Gloucester National Park|access-date=2 December 2017|publisher=[[National Trust of Australia]]}}</ref><ref name="Pemberton">{{cite web |title=Pemberton Bushwalks |url=https://images.impartmedia.com/pembertonvisitor.com.au/documents/BushwalksBook.pdf |publisher=Pemberton Visitor Centre |access-date=12 June 2020}}</ref>

Karri wood is a beautiful mahogany colour, lighter in colour than [[jarrah (tree)|jarrah]]. It is used extensively in the building industry, particularly in roofs for the length and knot-free quality of the boards. The wood is also used for flooring, furniture, cabinetry and plywood. The heartwood is golden to reddish brown, often with an orange or purple cast, and tends to darken with age. It has an interlocked grain with a uniform medium-coarse texture.<ref name=wood>{{cite web|url=http://www.wood-database.com/karri/|title=Karri|publisher=The wood database|access-date=2 December 2017}}</ref> It has the reputation of being termite-prone, although it is nowhere near as susceptible to these insects as pine. It is durable against rot. It is also an excellent furniture wood.

Some of the main streets of early Sydney were paved with blocks of Karri but have been long since covered by [[Asphalt concrete|asphalt]]. The wood was also sent to London for the same purpose.<ref name=Stanford/>

Karri honey is widely sought after for its clarity, light color and delicate flavor.<ref name=gardner/> In 1952 it was estimated that 25% of honey produced in Western Australia was produced in Karri forests.  Tourism to this area is also supported by the Karri. Main honey flows occur every four to five years with even larger flows every fifteen years or so.<ref name=gardner/>
